source_text:
Quare si uobis iam persuadetur posse aliquid boni omnipotentem deum de nihilo facere, uenite in catholicam et discite omnes naturas, quas fecit et condidit deus, excellentiae gradibus ordinatas a summis usque ad infimas, omnes bonas, sed alias aliis esse potiores, easque factas esse de nihilo, cum deus artifex per sapientiam suam potentialiter, ut ita dicam, operaretur, ut posset esse, quod non erat, et in quantum esset, bonum esset; in quantum autem deficeret, se non de deo genitum, sed ab ipso de nihilo factum ostenderet. quid enim uos teneat, si consideretis, non inuenitis, cum terram luminis, quam describitis, neque hoc esse, quod deus est, possitis dicere, ne in ipsam dei naturam foeditas quadrae illius inartetur; neque de illo genitam, ne nihilominus hoc, quod deus est, cogatur intellegi et ad eandem deformitatem redeat; nec alienam ab illo, ne in alieno regna eum posuisse et non duas, sed tres naturas dicere urgeamini; neque ab eodem de aliena factam substantia, ne aut bonum aliud fuerit . praeter deum, aut malum praeter gentem tenebrarum. remanet igitur uobis, ut de nihilo terram luminis deum fecisse fateamini, et non uultis credere. quodsi magnum aliquod bonum, quod tamen illo ipso esset inferius, deus ex nihilo facere potuit. potuit etiam, quia bonus est et nulli bono inuidet, facere alterum bonum, quod illo priore esset inferius; potuit et tertium, cui secundum praeponeretur, et deinde usque ad infimum bonum naturarum factarum ordinem ducere, donec uniuersitas earum non numero indefinito incerta difflueret. sed certo terminata consisteret. aut si nec de nihilo istam luminis terram deum fecisse uultis fateri, non erit exitus. quo tantas turpitudines et tam sacrilegas opiniones euadatis.
Aut uidete certe, quoniam liberum est carnali cogitationi phantasmata qualia libuerit opinari, ne forte possitis aliam quamcumque formam huic coniunctioni duarum terrarum inuenire. ne tam detestabilis et auersanda rerum facies animo occurrat, terram scilicet dei, siue Sit eiusdem naturae, qua deus est, siue diuersae, in qua tamen dei regna fundata sint, ita ingenti mole per inmensum iacere, ut per infinitum porrectis et apertis membris iaceat. quibus foedissime atque turpissime ab inferiore parte recipiat etiam ipsum inmensae magnitudinis inartatum illum cuneum terrae tenebrarum. sed quicquid aliud inueneritis figurae. quo duae istae terrae sibi coniungantur, delere profecto Manichaei litteras non potestis: non dico alias, quibus expressius ista descripsit — fortassis enim quia paucioribus notae sunt. minus periculi habere uideantur istas ipsas, de quibus nunc agitur, epistulae fundamenti, quae fere omnibus, qui apud uos inluminati uocantur, solet esse notissima. hic quippe ita scribitur: iuxta unam uero partem ac latus illius inlustris ac sanctae terrae erat tenebrarum terra profunda et inmensa magnitudine.
thought_title: Mani's land of light must be made from nothing
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, pressing them on the origin of the land of light described in Mani's Fundamental Letter.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore if it is now being persuaded to you that almighty God can make something good from nothing, come into the Catholic Church and learn that all natures, which God made and created, are ordered by degrees of excellence from the highest down to the lowest, all good, but some are more excellent than others, and that they were made from nothing, when God the artisan through his wisdom worked, so to speak, with power, so that what was not could come to be, and insofar as it existed, it would be good; but insofar as it fell short, it would show itself not begotten from God, but made by him from nothing. For what holds you, if you consider it, you do not find, since the land of light, which you describe, you cannot say is this, which God is, lest the foulness of that square be forced into the very nature of God; nor begotten from him, lest it be forced to be understood as this, which God is, and return to the same deformity; nor foreign to him, lest you be compelled to say that he placed his kingdoms in something foreign and that there are not two, but three natures; nor made by him from a foreign substance, lest there was either another good besides God, or an evil besides the nation of darkness. It remains therefore for you to confess that God made the land of light from nothing, and you do not want to believe it. But if God could make from nothing some great good, which nevertheless would be lower than he himself, he could also, because he is good and begrudges no good, make another good, which would be lower than that former one; he could also make a third, to which the second would be preferred, and then lead the order of created natures down to the lowest good, until the whole of them would not flow apart uncertain with an indefinite number, but would stand fixed with a certain limit. Or if you do not want to confess that God made this land of light even from nothing, there will be no way out by which you may escape such great foulnesses and such sacrilegious opinions. Or certainly see, since it is free for carnal thought to imagine whatever fantasies it pleases, whether perhaps you can find some other form for this joining of the two lands, lest so detestable and abhorrent a face of things occur to the mind, namely the land of God, whether it is of the same nature, which God is, or of a different one, in which nevertheless the kingdoms of God are founded, lying so with huge mass through the immense, that it lies with limbs stretched and spread through the infinite, by which limbs it receives most foully and most shamefully from the lower part that wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense magnitude, forced in. But whatever other figure you find, by which these two lands are joined to each other, you certainly cannot delete the writings of Mani: I do not say the others, in which he described these things more expressly — for perhaps because they are known to fewer people, they seem to have less danger — but these very ones, of the Fundamental Letter, about which we are now dealing, which is usually most known to nearly all, who among you are called enlightened. For here it is written thus: but along one part and side of that illustrious and holy land was the land of darkness, deep and of immense magnitude.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for Mani's realm of God.
Fixed glossary term for Mani's realm of evil.
Fixed glossary term for the doctrine that God made creatures from nothing.
Fixed glossary term for created kinds or essences.
Fixed glossary term for images formed in the mind from bodily sense experience.
Manichaean technical term for the elect, rendered literally to preserve the sect's self-designation.

pass_b_english: So if you are now persuaded that almighty God can make something good from nothing, come into the Catholic Church and learn that all the natures God made and established are arranged in ranks of excellence from the highest to the lowest, all of them good, but some better than others. They were made from nothing when God the craftsman worked through his wisdom with power, so to speak, so that what did not exist could come to exist, and insofar as it existed it was good; but insofar as it fell short, it showed that it was not begotten from God but made by him from nothing. If you think it through, you will find nothing that holds you back. For you cannot say that the land of light you describe is what God is, lest the foulness of that wedge be forced into God's own nature. You cannot say it was begotten from him, lest it likewise be understood to be what God is and fall back into the same deformity. You cannot say it is foreign to him, lest you be compelled to say he set up his kingdom in something foreign to him and to speak of not two but three natures. And you cannot say he made it from a foreign substance, lest there be some other good besides God or some evil besides the race of darkness. What remains, then, is for you to confess that God made the land of light from nothing—and you refuse to believe it. But if God could make from nothing some great good that was nevertheless lower than himself, then because he is good and begrudges no good thing, he could also make a second good lower than the first. He could make a third, ranked below the second, and so on down to the lowest good in the order of created natures, until the whole of them stood firm, fixed by a definite limit rather than flowing apart in an indefinite number, uncertain. Or if you refuse to confess that God made even that land of light from nothing, you will have no way out, no escape from such great foulness and such sacrilegious opinions.

Or at least consider this, since fleshly thought is free to imagine whatever fantasies it pleases: perhaps you can find some other shape for this joining of the two lands, so that such a detestable and abhorrent picture does not come to mind—the land of God, whether of the same nature as God or of a different one, in which God's kingdom is founded, lying stretched out in an immense mass through infinite space, so that it lies with its limbs extended and spread open through infinity, by which limbs, most foully and shamefully from below, it receives even that inserted wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size. But whatever other shape you find for how these two lands are joined together, you certainly cannot erase the letter of Mani. I do not mean the other letters in which he described these things more explicitly—perhaps because fewer people know them, they seem to carry less danger. I mean this very letter of the Foundation that we are now discussing, which is generally best known to nearly all those among you who are called enlightened. For here it is written: "Along one side and flank of that illustrious and holy land was the land of darkness, deep and of immense size."

problems.why: Praeponeretur means 'placed before/ranked above,' not 'preferred' as in liking; it's about hierarchy.
Certo terminata means 'fixed by a definite limit/boundary,' not 'bounded by a fixed number'; numerus is in the previous clause.
problems.ruling: Certo terminata = 'bounded by a fixed limit,' not 'number'; numero in prior clause already translated as 'number,' distorting meaning.

problems.quote: flowing apart in an indefinite, uncertain mass
problems.why: Numero indefinito goes with difflueret: 'flow apart in an indefinite number,' not 'mass.'
problems.fix: flow apart indefinite in number, uncertain
problems.ruling: Numero indefinito modifies difflueret: 'flow apart in indefinite number,' not 'mass'; English wrongly attaches 'number' to prior clause.

edits.new: the second would be ranked above it

edits.old: bounded by a fixed number rather than flowing apart in an indefinite, uncertain mass
edits.new: fixed by a definite limit rather than flowing apart in an indefinite number, uncertain

fixed: Changed 'preferred' to 'ranked above it' because 'praeponeretur' means placed before or ranked above, not preferred as in liking.
Changed 'bounded by a fixed number' to 'fixed by a definite limit' because 'certo terminata' means fixed by a definite limit, not a fixed number.

Changed 'flowing apart in an indefinite, uncertain mass' to 'flowing apart in an indefinite number, uncertain' because 'numero indefinito incerta difflueret' means flow apart in an indefinite number, uncertain.

problems.quote: to which the second would be ranked above it
problems.why: "cui secundum praeponeretur" means 'to which the second would be preferred/put before,' i.e., the second ranked above the third, not vice versa.
problems.fix: a third, to which the second would be preferred

problems.quote: lest the foulness of that square be forced into God's own nature
problems.source_quote: ne in ipsam dei naturam foeditas quadrae illius inartetur
problems.why: "quadrae" means "wedge," not "square" (quadrata). The wedge is the land of darkness forced into God.
problems.fix: lest the foulness of that wedge be forced into God's own nature
problems.ruling: quadrae here means wedge, not square; context confirms the wedge of darkness forced in.

problems.quote: and in its lower part receives, in the most foul and shameful way, that wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size, forced into it
problems.source_quote: quibus foedissime atque turpissime ab inferiore parte recipiat etiam ipsum inmensae magnitudinis inartatum illum cuneum terrae tenebrarum
problems.why: "quibus" refers back to "membris" (limbs), not "lower part." The limbs receive the wedge; "ab inferiore parte" means "from below."
problems.fix: by which limbs, most foully and shamefully from below, it receives even that wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size, forced in
problems.ruling: quibus refers to membris; limbs receive wedge from below, not lower part receiving it.

edits.old: to which the second would be ranked above it
edits.new: to which the second would be preferred

edits.old: lest the foulness of that square be forced into God's own nature
edits.new: lest the foulness of that wedge be forced into God's own nature

edits.old: and in its lower part receives, in the most foul and shameful way, that wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size, forced into it
edits.new: by which limbs, most foully and shamefully from below, it receives even that wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size, forced in

fixed: Fixed 'to which the second would be ranked above it' to 'to which the second would be preferred': source 'cui secundum praeponeretur' means the second is preferred/put before the third.
Fixed 'that square' to 'that wedge': source 'quadrae' means wedge, not square.

Fixed 'and in its lower part receives...' to 'by which limbs, most foully and shamefully from below, it receives...': source 'quibus' refers to 'membris' (limbs), and 'ab inferiore parte' means from below.

problems.why: Gens here means "race, people, kind"—the standard term for Mani's land of darkness as a collective entity. "Nation" is anachronistic and misleading.

problems.quote: to which the second would be preferred
problems.why: "praeponeretur" means "would be preferred to it," not "would be preferred." The third is preferred over the second, not vice versa.
problems.fix: a third, to which the second would be subordinated
problems.ruling: "cui secundum praeponeretur": the third is preferred to the second; English reverses the hierarchy, misleading the reader.

problems.why: "Inartatum" means "unshaped, formless, crude" (from in- + ars/artus), not "forced in." The wedge is shapeless/chaotic, not compelled.
problems.ruling: "inartatum" means unshaped/formless, not "forced in"; earlier "inartetur" is rendered "forced into," compounding the error.

edits.old: some evil besides the nation of darkness
edits.new: some evil besides the race of darkness

edits.old: He could make a third, to which the second would be preferred, and so on
edits.new: He could make a third, to which the second would be subordinated, and so on

edits.old: it receives even that wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size, forced in
edits.new: it receives even that unshaped wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size

fixed: gens tenebrarum: 'gens' here means race/people/kind, so 'race of darkness' is correct.
cui secundum praeponeretur: the third is preferred over the second, so 'to which the second would be subordinated' is correct.
inartatum: means unshaped/formless, not forced in; removed 'forced in' and added 'unshaped'.

problems.quote: that unshaped wedge of the land of darkness
problems.why: inartatum means inserted or fitted in, the same verb as inartetur, not unshaped.
problems.fix: that inserted wedge of the land of darkness
problems.ruling: 'inartatum' is the participle of the verb behind 'inartetur' (fitted in, inserted). 'Unshaped' invents a different meaning and breaks the link between the two words.

edits.old: it receives even that unshaped wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size.
edits.new: it receives even that inserted wedge of the land of darkness, itself of immense size.

fixed: Fixed 'unshaped wedge' to 'inserted wedge': source 'inartatum illum cuneum terrae tenebrarum' means fitted/inserted in (same verb as 'inartetur' above), not unshaped.

fixed.quote: to which the second would be subordinated
fixed.note: 'cui secundum praeponeretur' means the second is placed above the third, so 'subordinated' turns the order upside down, and the proposed fix repeats that mistake.

last_rejected.quote: worked through his wisdom with power, so to speak
last_rejected.source_quote: per sapientiam suam potentialiter, ut ita dicam, operaretur
last_rejected.why: potentialiter means potentially (the hedged technical adverb), not potently or with power.
last_rejected.fix: was at work through his wisdom, potentially, so to speak
last_rejected.ruling: 'potentialiter' with 'per sapientiam' and 'ut ita dicam' is a rare coinage; 'with power' is a loose but defensible reading of potentia, not a clear meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: lest it likewise be understood to be what God is and fall back into the same deformity
last_rejected.source_quote: ne nihilominus hoc, quod deus est, cogatur intellegi et ad eandem deformitatem redeat
last_rejected.why: The subject that is forced to be understood and falls back into deformity is what God is, not the land.
last_rejected.fix: lest what God is nonetheless be forced to be understood and fall back into the same deformity
last_rejected.ruling: Subject of 'cogatur intellegi' is the land (terram ... genitam); being begotten of God would make it 'hoc quod deus est'. English agency is correct.

last_rejected.quote: If you think it through, you will find nothing that holds you back.
last_rejected.source_quote: quid enim uos teneat, si consideretis, non inuenitis
last_rejected.why: Source: you do not find what could hold you (in your position); 'quid teneat' is an indirect question, not 'nothing holds you back'. Also the 'enim' reasoning is lost.
last_rejected.fix: For if you consider it, you cannot find what could hold you in place.
last_rejected.ruling: “non inuenitis quid…teneat” means you find nothing that could hold you; “holds you back” and dropped “enim” stay within normal range.
